stem: A client with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy is eating poorly because the family believes protein will worsen the encephalopathy. Which nursing teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Do not routinely restrict protein; provide adequate protein across small, frequent meals and include an early breakfast or late-evening snack to reduce prolonged fasting.
options.B: Reduce protein whenever encephalopathy symptoms appear, then restore the usual intake after mental status improves so less dietary nitrogen reaches the intestine.
options.C: Keep protein intake unchanged but space meals farther apart during the day, because longer fasting periods decrease ammonia production and protect cognition.
options.D: Prioritize sodium restriction before correcting poor protein intake and postpone extra meals or snacks until the encephalopathy has remained absent for several days.

rationale: Current AASLD guidance states that protein intake should not be restricted in clients with hepatic encephalopathy and recommends minimizing fasting with regularly spaced nutritional intake and an early breakfast and/or late-evening snack. AASLD also emphasizes malnutrition and muscle loss as important problems in cirrhosis. Therefore A is correct. B reflects an outdated protein-restriction approach that can worsen protein catabolism without improving the course of encephalopathy. C retains protein but deliberately prolongs fasting, which conflicts with AASLD nutrition guidance. D delays correction of poor intake and makes sodium restriction the priority even though nutritional counseling should be individualized and prolonged fasting should be minimized.
educational_objective: In cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, avoid routine protein restriction and reduce catabolic fasting by providing adequate protein through frequent intake and an early breakfast or late-evening snack.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
source_document_title: Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis; Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis
source_version_date: AASLD clinical resource current on the AASLD site in 2026; supporting outpatient-management resource published February 15, 2024 and current in 2026
source_locator: Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis > Intake Interventions — Macronutrients: protein intake should not be restricted in patients with hepatic encephalopathy; fasting time should be minimized with no more than 3–4 hours between nutritional intake during waking hours; an early breakfast and/or late-evening snack should be recommended. Earlier discussion: historical concern that protein worsens hepatic encephalopathy was not replicated; a randomized trial found greater protein catabolism with restriction without improved encephalopathy evolution. Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis > Malnutrition in Cirrhosis: protein intake should not be restricted in hepatic encephalopathy; minimize fasting; use an early breakfast and/or late-night high-protein snack.
source_claim_supported: AASLD guidance directly supports avoiding routine protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy and minimizing fasting through regular intake and an early breakfast or late-evening snack to support nutrition and muscle preservation in cirrhosis.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four teaching statements to remove the absolute-word cue and uniquely-long keyed answer while preserving the cirrhosis-nutrition construct. The revised distractors test realistic misconceptions about protein restriction, prolonged fasting, and delayed nutrition support.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy — protein intake and meal timing
audit_findings.stem: PASS — identifies poor intake driven by a specific family misconception and asks one nutrition-teaching decision.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects AASLD recommendations to avoid protein restriction and minimize fasting with regular intake and a late-evening or early-morning feeding opportunity; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — reducing protein may seem intuitive because ammonia is involved in encephalopathy, but AASLD specifically advises against routine protein restriction.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — maintaining protein is appropriate, but intentionally lengthening fasting conflicts with guidance aimed at reducing catabolism.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — sodium management can matter in cirrhosis, especially with ascites, but delaying correction of poor protein intake and prolonged fasting is not supported and makes the wrong priority for this stem.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only choice that correctly addresses both the protein misconception and the harmful prolonged-fasting pattern.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B restricts protein, C prolongs fasting, and D postpones indicated nutrition support while prioritizing a different dietary issue.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are tightly matched in length and clinical detail and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes evaluation of nutritional status, diagnosis-based dietary care, and nutrition-related interventions.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether temporary protein reduction during encephalopathy or longer meal spacing could be defensible; current AASLD guidance explicitly rejects protein restriction in HE and recommends minimizing fasting, leaving A uniquely best.
